zedes.c: ZEDES Lat. In the civil law. A house, dwelling, place of habitation, whether in the city or country. Dig. 30, 41, 5. In the country everything upon the surface of the soil passed under the term “ades."" Du Cange; Calvin. -

zedificare.c: ZEDIFICARE Lat. In civil and old Pnglish law. To make or build a house; to erect a building. Dig. 45. 1, 7, 7. Zdificare in tuo proprio solo non licet quod alteri noceat. 3 Inst. 201. To build upon your own land what may injure another is not lawful. A proprietor of land has no right to erect an edifice on his own ground, interfering with the due enjoyment of adjoining premises, as by overhauging ZZEDIFICATUM SOLO them, or by throwing water from the roof and eaves upon them, or by obstructing ancient lights and windows. Broom, Max. 369. Zdificatum solo solo cedit. What is built upon land belongs to or goes with land. Broom, Max. 172; Co. Litt. 4a. ZEdificia solo cedumt. Buildings: belong to [go with] the soll. Fleta, lib. 3, c. 2, § 12.

zedile.c: ZEDILE In Roman law. An officer who attended to the repairs of the temples and other public buildings; the repairs and cleanliness of the streets; the care of the weights and measures; the providing for funerals and games; and regulating the prices of provisions. Ainsw. Lex.; Smith, Lex.; Du Cange. -

zenilitumedictum.c: ZENILITUM EDICTUM In the Roman law. The Adilitian Edict; an edict providing remedies for frauds in sales, the execution of which belonged to the curule sediles. Dig. 21. 1. See Cod. 4, 58.

zefesn.c: ZEFESN In old English law. The remuneration to the proprietor of a domain for the privilege of feeding swine under the oaks and beeches of his woods.

zegroto.c: ZEGROTO Lat. Being sick or indisposed. <A term used in some of the older reports. “Holt egroto.” 11 Mod. 179.

zegylde.c: ZEGYLDE Uncompensated, unpaid for, unavenged. From the participle of exclusion, a, @, or ez, (Goth.,) and gild, payment, requital. Anc. Inst. Eng.

zel.c: ZEL A Norman French term signifying “grandfather.” It is also spelled “aieul” and “ayic.” Kelham. ZEquior est dispositio legis quam homimis. The disposition of the law is more equitable than that of man. 8 Coke, 152.

zequitas.c: ZEQUITAS In the civil law. Equity, as opposed to strictum or summum jus, (q. ©.) Otherwise called equum, equum bonum, @wquum et bonum, equum et justum. Calvin. ; ZEquitas agit im personam. Equity acts upon the person. 4 Bouv. Inst. n. 3783. Z2quitas est correctio legis goneraliter lates, qua parte deficit. Equity is the correction of that wherein the law, by reason of fits generality, is deficient. Plowd. 375. ZEquitas est correctio qusedam legi adhikita, quia ab ef abest aliquid propter generalem sine exceptione comprehensienem. Equity is a certain correction applied to law, because on account of its general comprehensiveness, without an exception, something is absent from it. Plowd. 467. 45 ZSNECIA ZEquitas est perfecta quedam ratio quse jus scriptum interpretatur et emen-~ dat; nulla scriptura comprehensa, sed solum in ver& ratione consistens. Equity is a certain perfect reason, which interprets and amends the written law, comprehended in no.writing, but consisting in right reason alone. Co. Litt. 24d. ZEquitas est quasi squalitas. Equity is as it were equality; equity is a species of equality or equalization. Co. Litt. 24. ZEquitas ignorantis opitulatur, oscitantiss nom item. Equity assists ignorance, but not carelessness. ZEquitas non facit jus, sed juri aurzilfatur. Equity does not make law, but assists law. Lofft, 379. Zzquitas mungquam contravenit leges. Equity never counteracts the laws. ZEquitas sequitur legem. Tquity follows the law. Gilb. 186. ZEquitas supervacua odit. Equity abhors superfluous things. Lofft, 282. ZEquitas uxoribus, liberis, creditoribug maxime favet. Equity favors wives and children, creditors most of all. ZZquum et bonum est lex legum. What is equitable and good is the law of laws. Hob. 224.

zequus.c: ZEQUUS Lat. Equal; even. A provision in a will for the division of the residuary estate ex equus among the legatees means equally or evenly. Archer v. Morris, 61 N. J. Eq. 152, 47 Atl. 278.

zera.c: ZERA or ERA. A fixed point of chronological time, whence any number of years is counted; thus, the Christian era began at the birth of Christ, and the Mohammedan era at the flight of Mohammed from Mecca to Medina. The derivatign of the word has been much contested. Wharton. Oe

zerarium.c: ZERARIUM Lat. In the Roman law. The treasury, (/fiscus.) Calvin. 228. Lat. In the Roman law. Money, literally, brass;) metallic money in general, including gold. Dig. 9, 2, 2, pr.; Id. 9, 2, 27,5; Id. 50, 16, 159. —ZEs alienum. A civil law term signifyin a debt; the property of another; borrowe money, as distinguished from @s suum, one’s own money.—ZEs suum. One's own money. In the Roman law. Debt; a debt: that which others owe to us, (quod alit nobis debent.) Dig. 50, 16, 213.

zesneoia.c: ZESNEOIA In old English law. Esnecy; the right gr privilege of the eldest ESTIMATIO CAPITIS 48 born. Spelman; Glany. lib. 7, c. 3; Fieta, lb. 2, c. 66, §§ 5, 6.

zestimatiocapitis.c: ZESTIMATIO CAPITIS In Saxon law. The estimation or valuation of the head; the price or value of a man. By the laws of Athelstan, the life of every man not excepting that of the king himself, was estimated ata certain price, which was called the were, or cestimatio capitis. Crabb, Eng. Law, ce. 4. ZEstimatio preteriti delicti ex postremo facto nunquam cresoit. The weight of a past offense is never increased by a subsequent fact. Bacon.

zetas.c: ZETAS Lat. In the civil law. Age. —Zitas infdntis proxima. The age next to infancy; the first Malt of the period of childood, (pueritta,) extending from seven years to ten and a half. The age next to puberty; the last half of the period of childhood, (pucritia,) - extending from = years oo ., half to fourteen. Inst. 3, 20,9; 4 BI. Com

zetateprobanda.c: ZETATE PROBANDA A writ which inquired whether the king’s tenant holding in chief by chivalry was of full age to receive his lands. It was directed to the escheater of the county. Now disused.

zetheling.c: ZETHELING In Saxon law. generally a prince of the blood. A noble;

zanja.c: ZANJA Span. A water ditch or artificial canal, and particularly one used for pure poses of irrigation. See Pico v. Colimas, 32 Cal. 578.

zanjero.c: ZANJERO Span. A water.commissioner or superintendent, or supervisor of an irrigation system. See Pico v. Colimas, 32 Cal. 578.

zealot.c: ZEALOT This word is commonly taken in a bad sense, as denoting a separatist from the Church of England, or a fanatic. Brown.

zealouswitness.c: ZEALOUS WITNESS An untechnical term denoting a witness, on the trial of a cause, who manifests a partiality for the side calling him, and an eager readiness to tell anything which he thinks may be of advantage to that side.

zeir.c: ZEIR O. Se. Year. “Zeir ahd day.” Bell.

zemindar.c: ZEMINDAR In Hindu law. Landkeeper. An officer who under the Mohammedan government was charged with the financial superintendence of the lands of a district, the protection of the cuitivators, and the renlization of the government’s share of its produce, either in money or kind.
